title: Euclid's theorem
text:
Euclid's theorem is a fundamental statement in number theory that asserts that there are infinitely many prime numbers. It was first proven by Euclid in his work Elements. There are at least 200 proofs of the theorem.


== Euclid's proof ==
Euclid offered a proof in his work Elements (Book IX, Proposition 20), which is paraphrased here.
Consider any finite list of prime numbers p1, p2, ..., pn. It will be shown that there exists at least one additional prime number not included in this list. Let P be the product of all the prime numbers in the list: P = p1p2⋅⋅⋅pn. Let q = P + 1. Since q is either prime or not:

If q is prime, then there is at least one more prime that is not in the list, namely, q itself.
If q is not prime, then some prime factor p divides q. If this factor p were in our list, then it would also divide P (since P is the product of every number in the list). If p divides P and q, then p must also divide the difference of the two numbers, which is (P + 1) − P or just 1. Since no prime number divides 1, p cannot be in the list. This means that at least one more prime number exists that is not in the list.
This proves that for every finite list of prime numbers there is a prime number not in the list. In the original work, Euclid denoted the arbitrary finite set of prime numbers as A, B, Γ.
Euclid is often erroneously reported to have proved this result by contradiction beginning with the assumption that the finite set initially considered contains all prime numbers, though it is actually a proof by cases, a direct proof method. The philosopher Torkel Franzén, in a book on logic, states, "Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes is not an indirect proof [...] The argument is sometimes formulated as an indirect proof by replacing it with the assumption 'Suppose q1, ..., qn are all the primes'. However, since this assumption isn't even used in the proof, the reformulation is pointless."


=== Variations ===
Several variations on Euclid's proof exist, including the following:
The factorial n! of a positive integer n is divisible by every integer from 2 to n, as it is the product of all of them. Hence, n! + 1 is not divisible by any of the integers from 2 to n, inclusive (it gives a remainder of 1 when divided by each). Hence n! + 1 is either prime or divisible by a prime larger than n. In either case, for every positive integer n, there is at least one prime bigger than n. The conclusion is that the number of primes is infinite.

=== Proof by construction ===
Filip Saidak gave the following proof by construction, which does not use reductio ad absurdum or Euclid's lemma (that if a prime p divides ab then it must divide a or b).
Since each natural number greater than 1 has at least one prime factor, and two successive numbers n and (n + 1) have no prime factor in common, the product n(n + 1) has more different prime factors than the number n itself. So the chain of pronic numbers 1 × 2 = 2 {2},    2 × 3 = 6 {2, 3},    6 × 7 = 42 {2, 3, 7},    42 × 43 = 1806 {2, 3, 7, 43},    1806 × 1807 = 3263442 {2, 3, 7, 43, 13, 139}, ...provides a sequence of unlimited growing sets of primes.

== Stronger results ==
The theorems in this section simultaneously imply Euclid's theorem and other results.


=== Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions ===

Dirichlet's theorem states that for any two positive coprime integers a and d, there are infinitely many primes of the form a + nd, where n is also a positive integer. In other words, there are infinitely many primes that are congruent to a modulo d.

'''Euclid's theorem''' is a fundamental statement in [[number theory]] that asserts that there are [[Infinite set|infinitely]] many [[prime number|prime]] numbers. It was first proven by [[Euclid]] in his work ''[[Euclid's Elements|Elements]]''. There are at least 200 proofs of the theorem.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Meštrović |first=Romeo |title=Euclid's theorem on the infinitude of primes: a historical survey of its proofs (300 B.C.--2022) and another new proof |date=2023-07-25 |class=math.HO |eprint=1202.3670}}</ref>

== Euclid's proof ==
Euclid offered a proof in his work ''Elements'' (Book IX, Proposition 20),<ref>James Williamson (translator and commentator), ''The Elements of Euclid, With Dissertations'', [[Clarendon Press]], Oxford, 1782, page 63.</ref> which is paraphrased here.<ref>{{citation |first=Oystein |last=Ore |title=Number Theory and its History |year=1988 |orig-year=1948 |publisher=Dover |page=65 }}</ref>

Consider any finite list of prime numbers ''p''<sub>1</sub>, ''p''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''p''<sub>''n''</sub>. It will be shown that there exists at least one additional prime number not included in this list. Let ''P'' be the product of all the prime numbers in the list: ''P'' = ''p''<sub>1</sub>''p''<sub>2</sub>⋅⋅⋅''p''<sub>''n''</sub>. Let ''q'' = ''P'' + 1. Since ''q'' is either prime or not:
* If ''q'' is prime, then there is at least one more prime that is not in the list, namely, ''q'' itself.
* If ''q'' is not prime, then some [[prime factor]] ''p'' divides ''q''. If this factor ''p'' were in our list, then it would also divide ''P'' (since ''P'' is the product of every number in the list). If ''p'' divides ''P'' and ''q'', then ''p'' must also divide the difference<ref>In general, for any integers ''a'', ''b'', ''c'' if <math>a \mid b</math> and {{tmath| a \mid c }}, then {{tmath| a \mid (b - c) }}. For more information, see [[Divisibility]].</ref> of the two numbers, which is (''P'' + 1) − ''P'' or just 1. Since no prime number divides 1, ''p'' cannot be in the list. This means that at least one more prime number exists that is not in the list.

This proves that for every finite list of prime numbers there is a prime number not in the list.<ref>The exact formulation of Euclid's assertion is: "The prime numbers are more numerous than any proposed multitude of prime numbers".</ref> In the original work, Euclid denoted the arbitrary finite set of prime numbers as A, B, Γ.<ref>{{citation |first=Victor J. |last=Katz |author-link=Victor J. Katz |title=A History of Mathematics – an Introduction |edition=2nd |publisher=Addison Wesley Longman |year=1998 |page=87 }}</ref>

Euclid is often erroneously reported to have [[proof by contradiction|proved this result by contradiction]] beginning with the assumption that the [[finite set]] initially considered contains all prime numbers,<ref>Michael Hardy and Catherine Woodgold, "Prime Simplicity", ''[[Mathematical Intelligencer]]'', volume 31, number 4, fall 2009, pages 44–52.</ref> though it is actually a [[proof by cases]], a [[direct proof]] method. The philosopher [[Torkel Franzén]], in a book on logic, states, "Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes is not an indirect proof [...] The argument is sometimes formulated as an indirect proof by replacing it with the assumption 'Suppose {{math|''q''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''q''<sub>''n''</sub>}} are all the primes'. However, since this assumption isn't even used in the proof, the reformulation is pointless."<ref>{{citation |first=Torkel |last=Franzén |author-link=Torkel Franzén |title=Inexhaustibility: A Non-exhaustive Treatment |year=2004 |publisher=A K Peters, Ltd |page=101 }}</ref>

=== Variations ===
Several variations on Euclid's proof exist, including the following:

The [[factorial]] ''n''! of a positive integer ''n'' is divisible by every integer from 2 to ''n'', as it is the product of all of them. Hence, {{nowrap|''n''! + 1}} is not divisible by any of the integers from 2 to ''n'', inclusive (it gives a remainder of 1 when divided by each). Hence {{nowrap|''n''! + 1}} is either prime or divisible by a prime larger than ''n''. In either case, for every positive integer ''n'', there is at least one prime bigger than ''n''. The conclusion is that the number of primes is infinite.<ref>{{cite book |title=Further Pure Mathematics |last1=Bostock |first1=Linda |last2=Chandler |first2=Suzanne |last3=Rourke |first3=C. |date=2014-11-01 |publisher=Nelson Thornes |isbn=9780859501033 |pages=168 |language=en }}</ref>

== Euler's proof ==
Another proof, by the Swiss mathematician [[Leonhard Euler]], relies on the [[fundamental theorem of arithmetic]]: that every integer has a unique prime factorization. What Euler wrote (not with this modern notation and, unlike modern standards, not restricting the arguments in sums and products to any finite sets of integers) is equivalent to the statement that<ref>Theorems 7 and their Corollaries 1 and 2 in: Leonhard Euler. {{lang|la|italic=no|[http://eulerarchive.maa.org/docs/originals/E072.pdf "Variae observationes circa series infinitas"]}}. {{lang|la|Commentarii Academiae scientiarum imperialis Petropolitanae}} 9, 1744, pp. 160–188. [https://scholarlycommons.pacific.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?filename=0&article=1071&context=euler-works&type=additional English translation]</ref>
<math display="block">\prod_{p\in P_k} \frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{p}}=\sum_{n\in N_k}\frac{1}{n},</math>
where <math>P_k</math> denotes the set of the {{mvar|k}} first prime numbers, and <math>N_k</math> is the set of the positive integers whose prime factors are all in <math>P_k.</math>

To show this, one expands each factor in the product as a [[geometric series]], and distributes the product over the sum (this is a special case of the [[Euler product]] formula [[Proof of the Euler product formula for the Riemann zeta function|for the Riemann zeta function]]). 
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
\prod_{p\in P_k} \frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{p}} & =\prod_{p\in P_k} \sum_{i\geq 0} \frac{1}{p^i}\\ & = \left(\sum_{i\geq 0} \frac{1}{2^i}\right) \cdot \left(\sum_{i\geq 0} \frac{1}{3^i}\right) \cdot \left(\sum_{i\geq 0} \frac{1}{5^i}\right) \cdot \left(\sum_{i\geq 0} \frac{1}{7^i}\right)\cdots \\ 
& =\sum_{\ell,m,n,p,\ldots \geq 0} \frac{1}{2^\ell 3^m 5^n 7^p \cdots} \\ & =\sum_{n\in N_k}\frac{1}{n}.
\end{align}
</math>

In the penultimate sum, every product of primes appears exactly once, so the last equality is true by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic. In his first corollary to this result  Euler denotes by a symbol similar to <math>\infty</math> the "absolute infinity" and writes that the infinite sum in the statement equals the "value" {{tmath| \log\infty }}, to which the infinite product is thus also equal (in modern terminology this is equivalent to saying that the partial sum up to <math>x</math> of the harmonic series diverges asymptotically like {{tmath| \log x }}). Then in his second corollary, Euler notes that the product 
<math display="block">\prod_{n\ge2} \frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{n^2}}</math>
converges to the finite value 2, and there are consequently more primes than squares. This proves Euclid's theorem.<ref>In his [[History of the Theory of Numbers]] (Vol. 1, p. 413) [[Leonard Eugene Dickson|Dickson]] refers to this proof, as well as to another one by citing page 235 of another work by Euler: ''Introductio in Analysin Infinitorum''. Tomus Primus. Bousquet, Lausanne 1748. [https://scholarlycommons.pacific.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1100&context=euler-works]. There (§ 279) Euler in fact essentially restates the much stronger Theorem 19 (described below) in the paper of his former proof.</ref>

[[File:Euler's infinity sign.svg|thumb|upright=0.4|class=skin-invert|Symbol used by [[Euler]] to denote infinity]]
In the same paper (Theorem 19) Euler in fact used the above equality to prove a much stronger theorem that was unknown before him, namely that the series 
<math display="block">\sum_{p\in P}\frac 1p</math>
is [[Divergence of the sum of the reciprocals of the primes|divergent]], where {{mvar|P}} denotes the set of all prime numbers (Euler writes that the infinite sum equals {{tmath| \log\log\infty }}, which in modern terminology is equivalent to saying that the partial sum up to <math>x</math> of this series behaves asymptotically like {{tmath| \log\log x }}).

== Erdős's proof ==

[[Paul Erdős]] gave a proof<ref name="Havil">{{cite book |last1=Havil |first1=Julian |title=Gamma: Exploring Euler's Constant |year=2003 |url=https://archive.org/details/gammaexploringeu00havi_882 |url-access=limited |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=0-691-09983-9 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/gammaexploringeu00havi_882/page/n51 28]–29}}</ref> that also relies on the fundamental theorem of arithmetic. Every positive integer has a unique factorization into a [[Square-free integer|square-free]] number {{math|''r''}} and a [[square number]] {{math|''s''<sup>2</sup>}}.  For example, {{math|1=75,600 = 2{{sup|4}} 3{{sup|3}} 5{{sup|2}} 7{{sup|1}} = 21 ⋅ 60{{sup|2}}}}.

Let {{mvar|N}} be a positive integer, and let {{mvar|k}} be the number of primes less than or equal to {{mvar|N}}. Call those primes {{math|''p''<sub>1</sub>, ... , ''p''<sub>''k''</sub>}}.  Any positive integer {{mvar|a}} which is less than or equal to {{mvar|N}} can then be written in the form
<math display="block">a = \left( p_1^{e_1} p_2^{e_2} \cdots p_k^{e_k} \right) s^2,</math>
where each {{math|''e''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is either {{math|0}} or {{math|1}}. There are {{math|2<sup>''k''</sup>}} ways of forming the square-free part of {{mvar|a}}.  And {{math|''s''<sup>2</sup>}} can be at most {{mvar|N}}, so {{math|''s'' ≤ {{sqrt|''N''}}}}.  Thus, at most {{math|2<sup>''k''</sup> {{sqrt|''N''}}}} numbers can be written in this form.  In other words,
<math display="block">N \leq 2^k \sqrt{N}.</math>
Or, rearranging, {{mvar|k}}, the number of primes less than or equal to {{mvar|N}}, is greater than or equal to {{math|{{sfrac|1|2}}log<sub>2</sub> ''N''}}.  Since {{mvar|N}} was arbitrary, {{mvar|k}} can be as large as desired by choosing {{mvar|N}} appropriately.

== Furstenberg's proof ==
{{main|Furstenberg's proof of the infinitude of primes}}

In the 1950s, [[Hillel Furstenberg]] introduced a proof by contradiction using [[point-set topology]].<ref>
{{cite journal
| last = Furstenberg | first = Harry | author-link = Hillel Furstenberg
| title = On the infinitude of primes
| journal = [[American Mathematical Monthly]]
| volume = 62
| year = 1955
| pages = 353
| doi = 10.2307/2307043
| jstor = 2307043
| issue = 5
| mr=0068566
}}</ref>

Define a topology on the integers {{tmath| \Z }}, called the [[evenly spaced integer topology]], by declaring a subset {{tmath| U \subseteq \Z }} to be an [[open set]] [[if and only if]] it is either the [[empty set]], {{tmath| \emptyset }}, or it is a [[union (set theory)|union]] of arithmetic sequences <math display="inline">S(a,b)</math> (for {{tmath| a \neq 0 }}), where
<math display="block">S(a, b) = \{ a n  + b \mid n \in \mathbb{Z} \} = a \mathbb{Z} + b. </math>

Then a contradiction follows from the property that a finite set of integers cannot be open and the property that the basis sets <math display="inline">S(a, b)</math> are [[clopen set|both open and closed]], since
<math display="block">\mathbb{Z} \setminus \{ -1, + 1 \} = \bigcup_{p \text{ prime}} S(p, 0)</math>
cannot be closed because its complement is finite, but is closed since it is a finite union of closed sets.

== Recent proofs ==

=== Proof using the inclusion–exclusion principle ===

Juan Pablo Pinasco has written the following proof.<ref>Juan Pablo Pinasco, "New Proofs of Euclid's and Euler's theorems", ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]'', volume 116, number 2, February, 2009, pages 172–173.</ref>

Let ''p''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''p''<sub>''N''</sub> be the smallest ''N'' primes. Then by the [[inclusion–exclusion principle]], the number of positive integers less than or equal to ''x'' that are divisible by one of those primes is

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
1 + \sum_{i} \left\lfloor \frac{x}{p_i} \right\rfloor - \sum_{i < j} \left\lfloor \frac{x}{p_i p_j} \right\rfloor & + \sum_{i < j < k} \left\lfloor \frac{x}{p_i p_j p_k} \right\rfloor - \cdots \\
& \cdots \pm (-1)^{N+1} \left\lfloor \frac{x}{p_1 \cdots p_N} \right\rfloor. \qquad (1)
\end{align}
</math>

Dividing by ''x'' and letting ''x'' → ∞ gives

<math display="block"> \sum_{i} \frac{1}{p_i} - \sum_{i < j} \frac{1}{p_i p_j} + \sum_{i < j < k} \frac{1}{p_i p_j p_k} - \cdots \pm (-1)^{N+1} \frac{1}{p_1 \cdots p_N}. \qquad (2) </math>

This can be written as

<math display="block"> 1 - \prod_{i=1}^N \left( 1 - \frac{1}{p_i} \right). \qquad (3) </math>

If no other primes than ''p''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''p''<sub>''N''</sub> exist, then the expression in (1) is equal to <math>\lfloor x \rfloor </math> and the expression in (2) is equal to 1, but clearly the expression in (3) is not equal to 1. Therefore, there must be more primes than  ''p''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''p''<sub>''N''</sub>.

===Proof using Legendre's formula===

In 2010, Junho Peter Whang published the following proof by contradiction.<ref>Junho Peter Whang, "Another Proof of the Infinitude of the Prime Numbers", ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]'', volume 117, number 2, February 2010, page 181.</ref>  Let ''k'' be any positive integer.  Then according to [[Legendre's formula]] (sometimes attributed to [[Alphonse de Polignac|de Polignac]])
<math display="block"> k! = \prod_{p\text{ prime}} p^{f(p,k)} </math>
where
<math display="block"> f(p,k) = \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^2} \right\rfloor + \cdots. </math>
<math display="block"> f(p,k) < \frac{k}{p} + \frac{k}{p^2} + \cdots = \frac{k}{p-1} \le k. </math>

But if only finitely many primes exist, then
<math display="block"> \lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{\left(\prod_p p\right)^k}{k!} = 0, </math>
(the numerator of the fraction would grow [[Exponential growth|singly exponentially]] while by [[Stirling's approximation]] the denominator grows more quickly than singly exponentially),
contradicting the fact that for each ''k'' the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator.

=== Proof by construction ===

Filip Saidak gave the following [[proof by construction]], which does not use [[reductio ad absurdum]]<ref>{{cite journal |title=A New Proof of Euclid's Theorem |url=http://fermatslibrary.com/s/a-new-proof-of-euclids-theorem |first=Filip |last=Saidak |date=December 2006 |journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]] |volume=113 |issue=10|pages=937–938 |doi=10.2307/27642094|jstor=27642094 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> or Euclid's lemma (that if a prime ''p'' divides ''ab'' then it must divide ''a'' or ''b'').

Since each natural number greater than 1 has [[Fundamental theorem of arithmetic|at least one prime factor]], and two successive numbers ''n'' and (''n'' + 1) have no prime factor in common, the product ''n''(''n'' + 1) has more different prime factors than the number ''n'' itself. So the chain of [[pronic number]]s {{br}}1 × 2 = 2 {2},    2 × 3 = 6 {2, 3},    6 × 7 = 42 {2, 3, 7},    42 × 43 = 1806 {2, 3, 7, 43},    1806 × 1807 = 3263442 {2, 3, 7, 43, 13, 139}, ...{{br}}provides a sequence of unlimited growing sets of primes.

=== Proof using the incompressibility method ===
{{see|Incompressibility method}}
Suppose there were only ''k'' primes (''p''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''p''<sub>''k''</sub>). By the [[fundamental theorem of arithmetic]], any positive integer ''n'' could then be represented as
<math display="block">n = {p_1}^{e_1} {p_2}^{e_2} \cdots {p_k}^{e_k},</math>
where the non-negative integer exponents ''e''<sub>''i''</sub> together with the finite-sized list of primes are enough to reconstruct the number. Since <math>p_i \geq 2</math> for all ''i'', it follows that <math>e_i \leq \lg n</math> for all ''i'' (where <math>\lg</math> denotes the base-2 logarithm).  This yields an encoding for ''n'' of the following size (using [[big O notation]]):
<math display="block">O(\text{prime list size} + k \lg \lg n) = O(\lg \lg n)</math> bits.
This is a much more efficient encoding than representing ''n'' directly in binary, which takes <math>N = O(\lg n)</math> bits. An established result in [[Lossless compression#Limitations|lossless data compression]] states that one cannot generally compress ''N'' bits of information into fewer than ''N'' bits. The representation above violates this by far when ''n'' is large enough since {{tmath|1= \lg \lg n = o(\lg n) }}.  Therefore, the number of primes must not be finite.<ref>{{citation |title=Kolmogorov complexity and algorithmic randomness|first=Alexander|last=Shen|publisher=AMS|year=2016|url=http://www.lirmm.fr/~ashen/kolmbook-eng.pdf|page=245}}</ref>

=== Proof using an even–odd argument ===
Romeo Meštrović used an even-odd argument to show that if the number of primes is not infinite then 3 is the largest prime, a contradiction.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Meštrović |first1=Romeo |title=A Very Short Proof of the Infinitude of Primes |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |date=13 December 2017 |volume=124 |issue=6 |page=562 |doi=10.4169/amer.math.monthly.124.6.562 |url=https://doi.org/10.4169/amer.math.monthly.124.6.562 |access-date=30 June 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Suppose that <math>p_1=2 < p_2 = 3 < p_3 < \cdots < p_k</math> are all the prime numbers. Consider <math>P=3p_3p_4\cdots p_k</math> and note that by assumption all positive integers relatively prime to it are in the set {{tmath|1= S=\{1, 2, 2^2, 2^3, \dots\} }}. In particular, <math>2</math> is relatively prime to <math>P</math> and so is {{tmath| P-2 }}. However, this means that <math>P-2</math> is an odd number in the set {{tmath| S }}, so {{tmath|1= P-2=1 }}, or {{tmath|1= P = 3 }}. This means that <math>3</math> must be the largest prime number which is a contradiction.

The above proof continues to work if <math>2</math> is replaced by any prime <math>p_j</math> with {{tmath| j \in \{1, 2, \dots, k-1\} }}, the product <math>P</math> becomes <math>p_1p_2\cdots p_{j-1}\cdot p_{j+1}\cdots p_k</math> and even vs. odd argument is replaced with a divisible vs. not divisible by <math>p_j</math> argument. The resulting contradiction is that <math>P-p_j</math> must, simultaneously, equal <math>1</math> and be greater than {{tmath| 1 }},{{efn|In the proof above (with {{tmath|1= j=1, p_j=2 }}), this contradiction would look as follows: {{tmath|1= 1=P-2>3p_k-2>2>1 }}. In the more general proof, the contradiction would be: {{tmath|1= 1=P-p_j>2p_k-p_j>p_j>1 }}; that is, <math>p_j</math> replaces <math>2</math> and the coefficient of <math>p_k</math> is the smallest prime in {{tmath| P }}.}} which is impossible.

== Stronger results ==

The theorems in this section simultaneously imply Euclid's theorem and other results.

=== Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions ===
{{main article|Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions}}

Dirichlet's theorem states that for any two positive [[coprime]] [[integer]]s ''a'' and ''d'', there are infinitely many [[prime number|primes]] of the form ''a'' + ''nd'', where ''n'' is also a positive integer. In other words, there are infinitely many primes that are [[congruence relation|congruent]] to ''a'' [[modular arithmetic|modulo]] ''d''.

=== Prime number theorem ===
{{main article|Prime number theorem}}

Let {{math|''π''(''x'')}} be the [[prime-counting function]] that gives the number of primes less than or equal to {{mvar|x}}, for any real number {{mvar|x}}. The prime number theorem then states that {{math|''x'' / log ''x''}} is a good approximation to {{math|''π''(''x'')}}, in the sense that the [[limit of a function|limit]] of the ''quotient'' of the two functions {{math|''π''(''x'')}} and {{math|''x'' / log ''x''}} as {{mvar|x}} increases without bound is 1:
<math display="block">\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty} \frac{\pi(x)}{x/\log(x)}=1. </math>

Using [[asymptotic notation]] this result can be restated as
<math display="block">\pi(x)\sim \frac{x}{\log x}.</math>

This yields Euclid's theorem, since <math>\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty} \frac{x}{\log x}=\infty. </math>

=== Bertrand–Chebyshev theorem ===

In [[number theory]], [[Bertrand's postulate]] is a [[theorem]] stating that for any [[integer]] {{tmath| n > 1 }}, there always exists at least one [[prime number]] such that
<math display="block">n < p < 2n.</math>
Equivalently, writing <math>\pi(x)</math> for the [[prime-counting function]] (the number of primes less than or equal to {{tmath| x }}), the theorem asserts that <math display="inline">\pi(x) - \pi(\tfrac{x}{2}) \ge 1</math> for all {{tmath| x \geq 2 }}.

This statement was first conjectured in 1845 by [[Joseph Louis François Bertrand|Joseph Bertrand]]<ref>{{citation |first=Joseph |last=Bertrand |author-link=Joseph Bertrand |title=Mémoire sur le nombre de valeurs que peut prendre une fonction quand on y permute les lettres qu'elle renferme. |journal=Journal de l'École Royale Polytechnique |issue=Cahier 30 |volume=18 |year=1845 |pages=123–140 |language=fr |url={{Google Books|WTa-qRIWckoC|page=123|plainurl=yes}}}}.</ref> (1822–1900). Bertrand himself verified his statement for all numbers in the interval {{nowrap|[2, 3 × 10<sup>6</sup>].}}
His conjecture was completely [[Proof of Bertrand's postulate|proved]] by [[Pafnuty Chebyshev|Chebyshev]] (1821–1894) in 1852<ref>{{citation |first=P. |last=Tchebychev |author-link=Pafnuty Chebyshev |title=Mémoire sur les nombres premiers. |journal=Journal de mathématiques pures et appliquées |series=Série 1 |year=1852 |pages=366–390 |url=http://sites.mathdoc.fr/JMPA/PDF/JMPA_1852_1_17_A19_0.pdf |language=fr}}. (Proof of the postulate: 371–382). Also see Mémoires de l'Académie Impériale des Sciences de St. Pétersbourg, vol. 7, pp. 15–33, 1854</ref> and so the postulate is also called the '''Bertrand–Chebyshev theorem''' or '''Chebyshev's theorem'''.
